#8611. Park Campsites Cost a Fraction of a Hotel Room – Book the Day Reservations Open

A campsite in a state or national park costs a fraction of a hotel room, but popular campgrounds can fill the day reservations open. Book on Recreation.gov or your state’s park reservation site that morning, buy an annual pass if you’ll visit several parks, and borrow gear for your first trip.

A tent site at Bryce Canyon National Park costs $30 a night, while U.S. hotel rooms averaged $160 a night in 2025, according to CoStar. For a seven-night trip, that’s $210 for the campsite against $1,120 for the room.

The hard part is getting the site, since some popular campgrounds can book up within minutes. Recreation.gov takes reservations for campgrounds in national parks, national forests, and other federal lands. Most of its campsites go on sale six months before arrival, usually at 10 a.m. Eastern. State park campsites book through each state’s own reservation site, on its own schedule, such as 120 days ahead in Minnesota.

For a trip just weeks away, look for campgrounds that take reservations only a short time ahead, such as Bryce Canyon’s Sunset Campground, which books no more than 14 days before arrival.

The America the Beautiful pass costs U.S. residents $80 and covers one car’s entrance and day-use fees for a year at national parks, national forests, and other federal lands, though not campsite fees. Three parks charging Yellowstone’s $35 a car would cost $105 in entrance fees, more than the $80 pass, so buy it when you’ll visit three or more. Some states sell their own park pass, such as Minnesota’s $35 year-round vehicle permit, which costs the same as five $7 day permits.

For a first trip, borrow or rent the tent and sleeping bags, and buy your own once you know you’ll go again. Or skip the tent and rent a camper cabin, which Minnesota’s state parks offer for $80 to $90 a night, about half the $160 average hotel rate.

Look up the date and hour your campground’s sites go on sale, on its Recreation.gov page under Seasons and Fees or on your state’s reservation site, and log in well before then.

#8610. Debbie App: Can This App Really Help You Pay Off Debt Faster?

Debbie is a debt payoff app built around a truth most people already understand but rarely see addressed in finance tools: paying off debt is not just about numbers, it is about behavior. And if behavior is the real challenge, motivation matters more than spreadsheets.

Most personal finance apps track balances and interest rates and then stop there. Debbie goes a step further by rewarding people for making progress. When you do the right things consistently, you do not just see your debt go down. You actually get something back.

Many debt payoff journeys fail in the same place. Not at the beginning, when motivation is high, but in the middle, when progress feels slow, and life gets in the way. Debbie is designed specifically for that phase.

After connecting your credit cards, student loans, or other debts, the app creates a personalized payoff plan based on your balances and payment history. The plan is realistic and focused on consistency rather than extreme sacrifices.

As you make payments and reduce balances, Debbie rewards you for that progress.

• Cash rewards• Gift cards• Partner offers tied to financial milestones

These rewards are not meant to eliminate debt on their own. They exist to reinforce the habit of showing up and sticking with the plan.

Debbie gives users a clean dashboard showing:

This reduces the mental stress of juggling multiple accounts.

Unlike most personal finance apps, Debbie pays users for progress, which helps reinforce positive habits. Over $2,319,961.65 earned by people reaching their money goals.

This makes it beginner-friendly, even for people new to budgeting or debt payoff.

Debbie works best for people who need accountability and encouragement. If you already know what to do but struggle to stay consistent, this app fills an important gap.

• Rewards that reinforce good financial behavior• A clean, easy to understand interface• A focus on progress instead of perfection• Motivation during the hardest part of the journey

There are also a few limitations to keep in mind. Debbie is not a replacement for a full budgeting system, and the rewards alone will not move the needle if you are carrying very large balances. You still have to do the work. The app simply makes it easier to keep going.

You will also need to link your financial accounts, which is standard for most modern finance apps but worth noting.

Debbie is a strong fit for people who feel overwhelmed by debt, burned out on traditional budgeting apps, or frustrated that they are doing the right things but still don’t feel any momentum.

If you are already highly disciplined and managing everything with detailed spreadsheets, you may not need the additional reinforcement. For most people, though, motivation is the missing piece.

Yes. Debbie is a legitimate personal finance app built around a behavior-driven debt payoff model. While it won’t magically erase debt, it helps users stay engaged, which is often the biggest missing piece in successfully paying off debt.

If you’re exploring Debbie, there are several other financial wellness and money-saving apps worth considering. Each app offers a different approach to helping users improve their finances, build better habits, or earn rewards.

Acorns automatically invests your spare change by rounding up purchases to the nearest dollar. It’s designed for beginners who want a simple, hands-off way to start investing.

Rocket Money focuses on budgeting, subscription tracking, and lowering monthly bills. It can help users identify recurring charges and negotiate certain expenses on their behalf.

Qapital combines budgeting with automated savings goals. Users can create custom “rules” that move money into savings automatically based on spending habits or milestones.

YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a purpose. It’s popular among people who want a more hands-on system for managing cash flow and paying off debt.

Paying off debt is rarely about knowledge. Most people already know what they should be doing. The real challenge is sticking with the plan month after month, even when progress feels slow.

Debbie helps solve that problem by rewarding progress, reinforcing positive habits, and making the journey feel less discouraging. It will not magically erase debt. But it can absolutely help you stay consistent long enough to change your financial life.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

Keep health insurance even if you’re young and healthy. One emergency, like appendicitis, can bring a hospital bill bigger than your savings, while a plan caps what you pay for covered care each year. If the premium is the problem, check your price after subsidies before you go without.

The premium is the cost you see each month. The bigger risk is a hospital’s list price, which is what patients without insurance are often billed.

In 2024, hospitals billed Medicare an average of about $63,550 for the least complicated appendix surgery stays and were paid about $10,800 in all, according to Medicare data. The typical family had $8,200 in checking, savings, and similar accounts in 2025, the Federal Reserve found.

A health plan lowers that bill in two ways. Say a 27-year-old on a bronze plan, the type that usually has the lowest premiums, needs her appendix out. An in-network hospital is paid the rate her insurer negotiated, not its list price, and her share of covered in-network costs stops at the plan’s out-of-pocket maximum. Federal rules cap that at $10,600 for one person this year, not counting premiums. Without a plan, she gets neither.

Going without can also cost you at tax time. California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia can add a penalty to residents’ income tax returns for months without coverage.

Price these first, since each can cut what coverage costs you:

Before you decide, preview plans for your area at HealthCare.gov or your state’s own Marketplace, and check whether your income qualifies you for a subsidy.

#8608. What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

Most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

For most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:

After three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

This is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

One of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

You do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

If you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single company’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small

Things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market

Research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That said, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

The key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

House-sitting gets you a free place to stay in exchange for caring for someone’s home and pets while they’re away. Join a house-sitting site and earn your first reviews on short sits near home, since owners choose sitters by their reviews. Then apply for longer sits whose dates and pets fit you.

A retired couple who would otherwise pay $120 a night for a room can save $5,040 with three two-week sits in England and France. After $259 for a year of TrustedHousesitters’ Premium plan, which a couple can share, they come out about $4,800 ahead.

The membership is the cheap part. Owners pick sitters by their reviews and references, so your first sit is the hardest to win, and TrustedHousesitters says having a reference doubles a sitter’s odds of landing a sit quickly.

TrustedHousesitters, the biggest site by its own count, charges $129 a year for Basic and $169 for Standard, plus a $12 booking fee per confirmed sit, or $259 for Premium with no booking fee. A smaller site, MindMyHouse, costs $29 a year. Ask a landlord or employer for a reference before your first application.

Read each listing’s routine before you commit, since a dog that needs three walks a day or a cat on insulin sets your daily schedule. Before the owners leave, get the vet’s details and agree on how vet bills get paid. TrustedHousesitters’ Standard and Premium plans add free calls with vets and an accident and liability plan for damage or injuries a pet causes while in your care. Premium can also pay toward a room within 20 miles of the home, up to $150 a night and $1,500 a sit, if an owner cancels 14 days or less before the sit starts.

You still pay to reach each sit, for food, and for lodging between sits. Abroad, you enter as a tourist, and border officers sometimes treat a sit as work, so TrustedHousesitters advises carrying a return or onward ticket and proof you can pay for the trip. Count your days, too, since a U.S. passport allows up to 90 days in any 180-day period across France and the rest of the Schengen area, Europe’s passport-free travel zone.

Start with two or three short sits within driving distance, and use their reviews to win the longer sits abroad.

#8605. What Are Mutual Funds?

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

Each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund company or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most important things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

For most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

When you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly

This is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

With thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

That said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most important step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

#8603. What Are Target Date Funds?

When you sign up for a 401(k) at work, there is a good chance that a target date fund shows up near the top of the investment options list. They are simple, widely available, and often the default choice for new investors. But simple does not always mean the best option for your situation.

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you plan to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”

The fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

The fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

This rebalancing happens automatically inside the fund, which is one reason they are so popular in workplace retirement plans. You do not need to log in and make adjustments. The fund does it for you.

The glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term plan for gradually reducing risk.

Different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

The important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending plans, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

The biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or company.

Over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

Because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

The glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

When you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

This is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

This approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

Even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your plan offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

But for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are currently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

#8602. Before a Medical Emergency, Save Your Out-of-Pocket Maximum and Sign a Health Care Proxy

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy. Keep savings equal to your health plan’s out-of-pocket maximum, and make sure disability coverage would replace part of your paycheck. Then sign a health care proxy and a HIPAA release so someone you trust can talk to your doctors and decide for you.

A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.

Most health plans cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a plan year for covered in-network care. It’s on page one of your plan’s Summary of Benefits and Coverage, called the out-of-pocket limit. Save that much.

Say a married couple’s family plan caps their share at $9,000 a year. They keep $9,000 in a health savings account, and each has signed a health care proxy naming the other to make medical decisions. When one has a heart attack, the account pays their share, and the proxy settles who decides. Without one, state law would usually pick the spouse, but a relative could contest that in court.

Keep that money in a health savings account if your plan qualifies, since the balance carries over and withdrawals for qualified medical bills are tax-free. If not, build it into your emergency fund with automatic deposits each payday. If illness keeps you out of work for months, disability insurance through your job or your own policy replaces part of your pay.

Sign your own proxy, also called a health care power of attorney, and a living will, which tells doctors what treatment you’d want if you can’t decide for yourself. One form, an advance directive, usually covers both. Add a HIPAA release, which names who can get your medical information, since some providers want permission in writing. Keep copies, with a list of your medications and doctors, where family can find them.

After a serious diagnosis, ask your insurer whether it offers a case manager, usually a nurse or social worker, to help coordinate your care. Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy, which can mean free or discounted care, so ask for the application before the first bill.

Start with the forms, since they cost little or nothing. CaringInfo posts every state’s advance directive form free, and you don’t need a lawyer. Give copies to the person you name and your doctor.

#8601. Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

By Deacon Hayes Updated November 14, 2026

If your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance company. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA plans, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health plan with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace plans are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing plan cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

The cheapest flight usually goes to the traveler who can shift dates or airports. Search a calendar of fares instead of fixed dates, include every airport near you, and set a price alert so you can book when the fare dips. Compare fares only after adding the bags and seat you’ll pay for.

Changing only your travel days can cut the fare. Google’s analysis of five years of its flight data found that leaving on a Monday and returning on a Tuesday or Wednesday costs about 14% less than flying on the weekend.

On Google Flights, open the date grid or price graph to see which travel dates around your trip have the lowest fares. Add every airport within an easy drive to the search, since a smaller airport nearby can be cheaper than your closest one. Also compare the round-trip fare with two one-way tickets on different airlines.

Say a family of four moves its departure from Saturday to Tuesday and flies from a smaller airport 40 minutes away, and each round-trip ticket costs $90 less. That’s $360 saved, minus gas for the longer drive.

Then turn on price tracking for the route, so Google emails you when the price changes significantly. Google’s analysis found domestic fares low from 22 to 57 days before departure and cheapest around 39 days out. International fares were low from 50 to 133 days out. For Thanksgiving or Christmas, book holiday flights in October instead of waiting for a sale.

Before you compare a basic economy or budget airline fare with a regular one, add the extras you’ll pay for. Basic economy, an airline’s most restricted ticket, usually limits bags and comes without a seat assignment. Google Flights’ bags filter adds checked or carry-on bag fees to the prices it shows. Add the cost of choosing a seat for each traveler who needs one.

Book the lowest total on the airline’s own site. The Transportation Department’s 24-hour rule covers tickets bought at least seven days before departure. Under it, the airline must either give a full refund on a ticket canceled within 24 hours or hold the fare for 24 hours without payment. Tickets bought through travel booking sites and agents aren’t covered.

Run your next fare search on Google Flights.

#8599. Solo Health Review (2026): Costs, Coverage, Pros & Cons

If you’re self-employed, finding affordable health coverage can be challenging. Traditional health insurance premiums can take a big bite out of your budget, especially when you’re paying for coverage without employer help.

Solo Health offers a different approach to health coverage designed specifically for entrepreneurs, freelancers, and self-employed business owners. Instead of purchasing a traditional individual health insurance policy, eligible business owners establish a self-funded major medical plan through their business.

But how does Solo Health work? Is the coverage comprehensive? And could it actually save you money? In this Solo Health review, we’ll break down the costs, benefits, potential drawbacks, and important details you should understand before enrolling.

Solo Health is a health coverage solution designed for self-employed individuals and business owners who want an alternative to traditional individual health insurance.

The company offers self-funded major medical plans that provide access to healthcare services through a nationwide PPO provider network.

Unlike a traditional insurance policy purchased through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace, Solo Health uses a business-based structure.

Your business establishes its own self-funded health plan to cover eligible medical claims.

According to Solo Health, its plans include:

One of Solo Health’s biggest selling points is major medical coverage specifically designed for self-employed people.

However, Solo Health is not a traditional ACA Marketplace insurance policy, and eligibility depends on a health questionnaire.

Solo Health operates differently from both traditional health insurance and healthcare-sharing programs. Instead of purchasing an individual insurance policy, your business establishes a self-funded health plan.

That self-funded plan pays eligible medical claims under the terms of your plan documents.

Here’s a simplified overview of how it works:

Preventive care is generally covered without meeting your deductible.

Prescription medications have their own coverage rules, including copays after the deductible.

Solo Health describes its product as a self-funded major medical health plan, not a healthcare-sharing ministry or a conventional individual insurance policy.

Eligible medical claims are paid through your business’s self-funded health plan.

While Solo Health provides major medical benefits, you should not assume it has all the same eligibility protections, regulatory requirements, or consumer safeguards as an ACA-compliant individual insurance policy.

For example, Solo Health requires applicants to complete a health questionnaire and meet its participation requirements. This differs significantly from ACA Marketplace plans, which generally cannot reject applicants because of preexisting medical conditions.

Before enrolling, make sure you understand the plan documents, coverage exclusions, and how the plan pays medical claims.

Solo Health offers several key medical benefits designed to protect members from both routine healthcare expenses and larger medical bills.

Here’s a closer look at what is included.

Solo Health covers eligible preventive healthcare services at 100%, with no deductible required.

This can be particularly helpful for self-employed individuals who want to stay on top of their health without paying the full cost of every preventive appointment. However, diagnostic tests or treatments performed during a preventive visit may be billed differently.

Solo Health covers primary care physicians and medical specialists. Members can access participating providers through the MultiPlan PHCS network, now associated with Claritev.

You generally don’t need a referral to see a specialist. For most non-preventive visits, you’ll pay the applicable cost until you meet your deductible. After you meet your deductible, the plan covers eligible medical services at 100%, subject to plan terms.

One of the most important reasons to have health coverage is protection against unexpected medical emergencies. A serious accident, hospitalization, or surgery can result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills.

According to the company, emergency services are processed as in-network regardless of which hospital provides the care.

Certain planned hospital admissions and surgeries require prior authorization.

Solo Health covers eligible mental health and substance use treatment. This can include outpatient therapy and other qualifying services. However, limits apply.

For example, Solo Health limits outpatient mental health therapy to 40 visits per covered individual each year. Some mental health treatments may also require prior authorization. If you regularly use mental health services, review these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health includes prescription benefits administered through FairosRx. Preventive medications in Tier 1 are covered at $0. For other covered medications, members generally pay the discounted cost until they meet their deductible.

Afterward, prescription copays apply based on the medication’s tier. Some specialty medications can still involve high out-of-pocket costs.

Solo Health also lists maternity and newborn care among its covered benefits. This can include eligible prenatal services, childbirth, and medical care for newborns.

However, anyone planning to start or expand a family should review the plan’s maternity provisions, eligibility requirements, and applicable exclusions before enrolling. Don’t assume every pregnancy-related service will automatically qualify for payment.

One of the biggest questions when considering any health coverage option is how much you’ll pay. Solo Health offers three plan designs, each with a different deductible.

The main difference between these plans is how much you must pay toward eligible medical expenses before the plan pays most covered costs at 100%.

All three plans offer the same core coverage and provider network. The deductible you select influences your monthly payment. Generally speaking, plans with lower deductibles cost more per month, while plans with higher deductibles cost less.

Your actual monthly cost depends on factors such as your age, location, household composition, and eligibility. Because pricing is individualized, the best way to determine your cost is to request a quote directly from Solo Health.

Let’s say you choose the Solo Health plan with a $5,000 individual deductible. You would generally pay the applicable cost of eligible non-preventive healthcare services until you’ve spent $5,000 toward your deductible.

After that, the plan pays 100% of eligible medical expenses for the remainder of the plan year. However, prescription copays and potential out-of-network charges can still apply.

This is why it’s important to understand the difference between your deductible and your total possible healthcare expenses.

Solo Health advertises its deductible as the out-of-pocket maximum for eligible medical care.

This structure can make medical expenses easier to plan for.

However, the advertised maximum may not cover every expense you could incur.

Prescription copays, excluded services, and charges above the plan’s out-of-network reimbursement amount may result in additional costs.

The major phone carriers discount their plans for employees of partner companies, union members, students, the military, first responders, teachers, nurses, and customers 55 and older. Find your group on your carrier’s discount page, verify once, and compare the discounted price with a cheaper plan before you sign up.

None of these discounts shows up on your bill on its own. The carrier charges full price until you sign up and prove you qualify.

Some take a percentage off a regular plan. AT&T’s discount programs take up to 20% off, depending on the plan, for employees of partner companies, union members, students, the military, veterans, and teachers. T-Mobile Work Perks takes 15% off for employees of participating employers, and Verizon’s discounts take 10% off for the military, first responders, nurses, teachers, and students.

Others are separate plans for one group, with their own prices and line limits. T-Mobile’s military and first responder plans cover as many as 12 lines, while its 55+ plans stop at two. AT&T’s 55+ plan allows up to 10 lines, though it saves the most on two.

To claim one, sign up on your carrier’s discount page and prove you qualify. Verizon confirms you belong to one of those groups through ID.me, an online identity service. AT&T asks for proof such as a pay stub or a DD-214 discharge form, and T-Mobile’s 55+ plans ask for a driver’s license or another government ID.

Ask what it combines with before you switch plans. Verizon won’t combine its military, first responder, nurse, teacher, and student discounts with one another, and AT&T’s 55+ plan can’t be combined with its discounts for veterans, teachers, nurses, or physicians. The discounted prices the carriers advertise also assume you pay by AutoPay.

Then check what it saves. A retired couple in their 60s paying by AutoPay for two lines on T-Mobile’s T-Mix More owes $130 a month. The plan’s 55+ version costs $120 and keeps the same four Picks, which you spend on perks such as Apple TV. That saves the couple $120 a year.

Before you sign up, price the same number of lines on a prepaid plan on the same network. The difference between that price and your discounted one is what the big carrier’s perks cost you.

To find a cheaper plan to weigh against your discounted price, compare the best cheap cell phone plans.

Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

The booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. #8595. 15 Active Jobs for People Who Hate Sitting – Weigh Pay Against Physical Toll

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Plenty of jobs pay you to walk, lift, and climb instead of sitting, and some pay well above the typical U.S. wage. Before you switch, compare each job’s pay and training with what it asks of your body, since the active jobs you can start fastest tend to pay the least.

Picture an office worker who trades her desk for a mail route. She now spends most of her shift on her feet, and the exercise she used to pay a gym for comes with the job.

The difference shows up in calories. The Compendium of Physical Activities, a research list rating how much energy activities take, scores each one against sitting quietly, which burns about 1 calorie an hour for every 2.2 pounds you weigh. For a 160-pound person, that puts an hour of office work at about 110 calories, delivering mail on foot at about 170, general yard work at about 290, and firefighting at about 580.

Carriers on walking routes cover about 4 to 12 miles a day and spend up to about six hours on foot, the National Association of Letter Carriers says. Over those six hours, a 160-pound carrier burns roughly 350 more calories than she would at a desk. The 15 jobs below run from that kind of steady walking to heavy lifting, and their pay ranges just as widely.

Pay below is each job’s May 2025 median from the Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), meaning half of workers in the job earn more and half less. For comparison, the median for all U.S. workers was $50,980.

The quickest jobs to start mostly pay the least. Animal care, grounds work, material moving, construction labor, and fitness training take little or no schooling, and all five pay under the $50,980 national median. Mail carriers are the exception. The other better-paid jobs here typically start with a training program, a degree, or an apprenticeship.

Physical work also brings more injuries than a desk job. BLS counts construction laborers, material movers, and flight attendants among the occupations with the highest injury and illness rates, and nurses and therapist assistants who lift patients are prone to back injuries.

The strain adds up with age. A University of Michigan Retirement and Disability Research Center study found that workers in more physically demanding jobs are more likely to be retired at any given age. The effect showed up almost entirely in men and was larger among those without a college degree. That makes saving early matter more in a heavy job, since your working years may be fewer.

To earn while you train, start with the trades. Electricians and elevator installers learn through apprenticeships that pay for their hours on the job, and carpenters can train the same way. The Labor Department’s Apprenticeship Finder lets you search openings by career and location.

#8594. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder.  And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me)

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.
